transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-11
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Sanjay Rao (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (AeroNova CTO), Liam Ortiz (AeroNova ML Eng), Priya Singh (AeroNova Infra)

Auto-generated Summary:
- Redwood demo focused on edge-case behavior under long-context (40k+ tokens) sessions, sustained high TPS, and streaming backpressure/timeouts.
- Discussed SLA guardrails, canary fallback strategies, batching/cache levers from Redwood Optimize, and Private deployment considerations for egress control.
- Next steps: perf spreadsheet, week-of benchmark, security docs.

Topics:
- long context architecture and kv cache eviction
- streaming chunking, backpressure, client timeouts
- routing to quantized lower-cost variants under load
- SLA guardrails and alerting in Console

Action items (captured verbally):
- See action_items field

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): ok hey thanks everyone for joining, i'm Alex Park from Redwood, i'll kick off, quick agenda — demo edge cases: long context + sustained load + streaming quirks, then canary/fallback patterns, then Q&A.
[00:18] Maya (AeroNova): yep thanks Alex, we are mostly concerned with two things: one is long-doc summarization flows where the context can be 30 to 50k tokens, and two is spikes — when our ingest service does bursts up to 3k reqs/sec so we want predictable p95s, right.
[00:35] Sanjay (Redwood): understood — a couple of quick clarifying q's: what's your p95 target today and do you have a hard timeout on the client side? also are you planning hosted or private?
[00:50] Liam (AeroNova): we aim for p95 under 500ms for the small assistant calls, for the long-doc flows it's acceptable to be 2 to 5 seconds but we don't want silent truncation. Client timeout is usually 15s. We're thinking private (VPC) for data residency but we'd consider dedicated capacity.
[01:12] Alex: perfect, we'll show how Redwood's streaming interacts with client timeouts and how the console surface SLA guardrails. Sanjay will start the console demo — he'll intentionally push a synthetic workload after the long-context run so you can see fallbacks.
[01:28] Sanjay: ok loading the model catalog — i'm selecting a 70B open-arch model we've onboarded and a 8k quantized variant for fallback. note — naming in the catalog is sometimes abbreviated in the UI, apologies if labels look different on your console.
[02:05] Sanjay: first demo — long context handling: i'm uploading a 42k-token doc, then we'll run a chat session that references earlier sections so we exercise KV cache retention and prefix caching.
[02:22] [clipper noise] Speaker 1: um this is the part where k v cache sometimes gets dropped if the prefix exceeds, like, the windowing heuristic —
[02:35] Sanjay: yeah good point — in our runtime we keep a rolling KV cache across segments and we have eviction policies that are workload-aware, there's also an option to pin prefixes for a session which avoids eviction for critical tokens, that helps summarization flows.
[02:58] Maya: when you say pin prefixes, is that a per-request header or a session flag?
[03:06] Sanjay: session flag — API accepts session metadata and in Console you can flip pin-prefix on per-route. behind the scenes it uses prefix hints to keep KV above the eviction threshold.
[03:27] Liam: what's the memory impact? we already have memory pressure on the host.
[03:34] Sanjay: it increases memory footprint linearly with pinned tokens, but Optimize suggests quantization + smaller attention windows for older segments; you'll see a recommendation in the Optimize tab after we run the replay.
[03:55] [00:04:00] Sanjay: ok starting chat, streaming on — you should see chunked tokens coming through. i'm going to artificially throttle network to simulate mobile clients.
[04:12] [00:06:10] Liam: tokens are arriving fine but the last chunk got delayed and the client fired a 15s timeout; the server kept generating — the client showed aborted but the server continued in the logs.
[04:30] Sanjay: this is the streaming backpressure issue — if the client disconnects, Redwood runtime supports 'graceful abort' and 'continue-in-background' policies. by default for hosted we do graceful abort after a short grace window; for Private you can configure 'continue' to persist generation and store output in object storage for retrieval.
[04:58] Maya: dangerous if it keeps consuming GPU after client disconnects though.
[05:06] Sanjay: agreed — that's why guardrails exist: you can set max-background-gens-per-session and per-tenant caps; Console exposes 'idle generation timeout' and 'bg generation CPU/GPU budget' counters so infra can alert before cost spikes.
[05:30] Alex: also we have routing policies — you can route by latency SLO or cost. under burst, we can route non-critical low-priority requests to quantized variants or to Dedicated reserved pool with higher latency but cheaper tokens.
[05:49] [00:08:12] Liam: curious about partial responses — can Redwood emit partial JSON or function-calls mid-stream reliably when there's backpressure?
[05:58] Sanjay: yes, streaming supports structured deltas and function-call mid-stream. caveat: if client disconnects mid-function-call you may get partial function payload; we recommend idempotent handlers and sequence identifiers so the app can reconcile.
[06:18] [00:09:30] Speaker 2: hmm the transcript messed that one up earlier — sometimes 'function call' became 'function call out' in the auto-caption.
[06:26] Sanjay: (laughs) yeah transcription hiccups — but the behavior stands. next i'm going to run a sustained TPS test at 2.5k rps to show autoscaling and backpressure behavior.
[06:42] [00:11:00] Sanjay: kicking off synthetic spike — note this is staging, not your prod account; Console will show per-route queue depth, batch sizes, and per-GPU concurrency.
[06:58] [00:12:05] Maya: i see the queue spike to ~200 and p95 rose to 1.8s, then you triggered fallback?
[07:07] Sanjay: yes, we set routing policy to 'latency-first' with cost-fallback. when p95 crosses 1.2s, traffic gradually shifts to quantized variant and to dedicated pool, which keeps critical SLOs for priority routes.
[07:23] Alex: important nuance — we don't drop traffic abruptly; it's a gradual shift with canary steps to avoid flapping and to keep KV cache warm for active sessions.
[07:39] Liam: how are you measuring p95 — is that end-to-end including network and client timeout?
[07:46] Sanjay: it's server-side p95 measured from request arrival to first byte served; Console can also show end-to-end metrics if you forward client-side telemetry via our ingestion SDK.
[08:05] Priya: about timeouts — we have a hard gateway timeout at 30s, if server-side generation keeps going beyond we will get killed at gateway. how do you handle long generations that need more than 30s?
[08:19] Sanjay: two patterns: 1) chunked progressive summaries — generate in sections and checkpoint results, 2) background generation with storage pull — produce to object store and notify client via webhook when ready. background mode requires explicit budget guardrails.
[08:36] Maya: what about cost control — we have budget constraints and worried about runaway background jobs.
[08:43] Alex: Optimize gives cost estimates per-route and per-model; you can set soft/before-billing alerts and hard caps that stop background gens when budget exceeded. We typically see customers combine quantized models with prefix pinning for long-doc to reduce both latency and cost.
[08:59] [00:14:00] Sanjay: ok i'm now enabling live traces — you can see traces per-token in the Console, the batcher shows average batch size decreased during the spike, which increases per-token cost but reduces latency.
[09:17] Liam: any recommended batcher tuning for high TPS short-context vs long-context flows?
[09:24] Sanjay: yes — for short-context high-tps, use continuous batching with small max batch sizes and low latency SLO. For long-context, favor larger batches and prefix caching; Optimize will propose a split route: short-context to latency-optimized pool, long-context to cost-optimized pool.
[09:44] Maya: when you say split route, is the decision per-request header-based?
[09:50] Sanjay: you can do it per-request via headers or via route rules that look at payload size/token-estimate. We have route templates in Console. We'll share an example rule in the perf sheet.
[10:08] [00:20:00] Alex: quick pause — any questions before the deeper perf notes and logs?
[10:15] Maya: just one — in private deployments how different is the default behavior around backpressure? we need more control in VPC.
[10:22] Sanjay: in Private, you get the control plane but most runtime knobs are exposed to your infra. default behavior is conservative (graceful abort) but you can override to permit background gens, tune eviction policies, and set stricter budget caps; Redwood support helps with tuning during onboarding.
[10:39] Priya: about auditability — do background gens show up in audit logs and cost attribution per team?
[10:45] Alex: yes — every generation has trace id, session id, and cost attribution. Console exposes per-team cost dashboards and you can export raw event logs to your SIEM.
[10:58] [00:25:00] Sanjay: now i'll show a failure scenario — i'm going to simulate a model OOM on a long-context session to show graceful degradation. starting the run...
[11:15] [00:26:30] Liam: saw an OOM and then a 502 to the client, did the runtime do an automatic retry?
[11:23] Sanjay: depending on state, we attempt R-s-try-with-backoff if the request is idempotent; for chat with session state we usually fail-open to fallback model rather than retrying to avoid duplicate outputs. Console shows the fallback event and the model used.
[11:42] Maya: is the fallback deterministic — customers worry about content drift.
[11:48] Sanjay: not strictly deterministic; fallback can change response shape. we surface 'regression risk' flags when falling back to quantized/smaller models — Optimize will show likely F1/semantic loss estimate so you can set auto-rollback thresholds.
[12:10] [00:32:00] Alex: let's talk SLO guardrails — customers often want a hard SLA for certain routes and relaxed for others. our policy engine allows per-route SLOs with actions on violation: alert, route-shift, throttle, or fail-closed.
[12:29] Maya: can we configure to drop non-critical telemetry and keep assistant responses under sla?
[12:35] Sanjay: yes — you can set priority queues and drop low-priority requests when queues exceed threshold. The Console will log drop events with reason codes for audit.
[12:50] Priya: for compliance: does ongoing background generation store content encrypted at rest and is KMS integration supported?
[12:57] Alex: yes to both — private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and we store outputs encrypted with per-tenant keys; we also provide redact hooks if you need to strip PII before storage.
[13:10] [00:40:00] Sanjay: i'm wrapping up with the Optimize recommendations — after the replay runs, Optimize produced suggestions: 1) quantize older segments to 4-bit for long-doc workflows, 2) enable prefix-pin for sessions with repeated access, 3) split routing rule based on token_estimate header.
[13:33] Maya: helpful — can you share the actual expected cost delta numbers?
[13:38] Alex: yes — that's in the perf spreadsheet Alex will send: expect ~40% token-cost reduction with quantization + prefix-pin in our tests for a 42k doc summarization flow, with p95 improving slightly due to less memory thrash.
[13:58] Liam: final q: what's the recommended test harness for us — load vs realism?
[14:05] Sanjay: we recommend two passes: synthetic spike tests (uniform payloads) to validate autoscaling/backpressure and replay-based tests using production traces for cache/kv behavior; we'll run a mixed test in the benchmark session.
[14:22] Alex: ok quick recap and next steps — we'll send the perf sheet, schedule the week-of benchmark, and share SAML + SOC2 checklist. anything to add?
[14:34] Maya: please include example route rules and console screenshots of the guardrail toggles.
[14:40] Alex: will do. thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links.

End transcript.

Meeting close: 16:12 PDT
